intro.text: Illustrations and calculations: This guide contains 46 numbered illustrations. The COCOMO worked example and cost-driver adjustment are presented as editable calculation tables, not illustrations, so the formula and arithmetic can be checked directly.

blocks.text: Six responsibilities of the software project manager

rows: Main point of contact between clients and dev team
Form and manage the dev team

blocks.text: The project manager ensures timely delivery within cost.

blocks.caption: Figure 1. Uncoordinated work compared with coordinated software delivery.
Figure 2. The manager connects six ongoing responsibilities.

blocks.text: Client communication, team formation and technical decisions

The project manager acts as the product owner — the point of interface between customers/stakeholders and the development team, ensuring the customer's requirements are addressed. She creates the team, finding the right people and putting them on the right tasks, then manages the team so the project moves towards timely completion. For a technology decision with multiple options, she consults team members and experts outside the team.

blocks.caption: Figure 3. Two-way exchange among stakeholders, manager and technical team.

blocks.text: Risk and configuration management
Some people may leave the team, so backup plans are needed — anticipate risks early and have a mitigation plan: plan A, plan B, plan C — so the impact on deliverables is minimised.

Configuration management: which tools, documentation etc. are required to combine all the modules so the customer can use the system; also accounting for changes — e.g. a developer creating a new version of the code — and managing different versions of the system.

blocks.caption: Figure 4. A high-level project workflow with continuous supporting management activities.

blocks.text: Plan and Document and Agile perspectives

Plan and Document aims to make software engineering predictable in budget and schedule. Agile does not try to predict cost and schedule at the start; it works with customers in frequent iterations and agrees on a range of time for best effort. User stories are rated by difficulty and assigned points, and points completed per iteration are recorded — a more realistic estimate of time and effort.

blocks.caption: Figure 5. Upfront planning contrasted with iterative planning and feedback.

blocks.text: Why estimation matters
Project estimation helps establish cost, establish a schedule and bid for projects. More detailed information about the project leads to more accurate estimates.

blocks.caption: Why estimate a project? Establish cost, establish schedule and bidding for projects.
blocks.alt: Why estimate a project? Establish cost, establish schedule and bidding for projects.

blocks.text: Software size and person-months
Lines of Code (LOC) measure software size. A KLOC is 1,000 lines of code; 4,000 LOC = 4 KLOC.

blocks.caption: Figure 7. KLOC counts estimated code, whereas effort measures work.

blocks.text: A person-month is the amount of work done by one person in one month. 12 PM = 12 × 1 = 4 × 3 = 2 × 6: 12 people for 1 month, 4 people for 3 months, or 2 people for 6 months.

blocks.caption: Figure 8. Three simplified ways of allocating 12 person-months of effort.

blocks.text: Work is expressed in person-months because it is easier to get a feel for how many people are needed to finish the work in a fixed time.
Empirical estimation versus heuristic estimation
Empirical estimation uses experience and educated judgement. Heuristic estimation uses mathematical relationships between parameters such as size and effort.

blocks.caption: Figure 9. Experience-based and model-based approaches to effort estimation.

blocks.text: Expert judgement
An expert makes an educated guess about the problem size after analysing the problem thoroughly, estimates the cost of the different components, and combines them into an overall estimate.

blocks.caption: Expert judgement: analyse, estimate components, combine.
blocks.alt: Expert judgement: analyse, estimate components, combine.

blocks.text: Drawbacks of expert judgement

rows: Even more so to win a contract
Overlooking factors / lack of adequate knowledge
Strong in database and UI, weak on additional modules or plugins

blocks.text: Solved by a group of experts? To an extent — but the group can still be biased, and decisions may be dominated by overly assertive or senior members.

blocks.caption: Expert-judgement drawbacks: individual bias, optimism, overlooked factors and group dominance.
blocks.alt: Expert-judgement drawbacks: individual bias, optimism, overlooked factors and group dominance.

blocks.text: Delphi estimation: anonymous repeated rounds

A coordinator gives each expert the SRS and an estimation form. Each expert estimates independently and submits their result to the coordinator. The coordinator summarizes the responses without identifying their authors and distributes the summary back to the experts.

blocks.caption: Figure 12. Five-stage Delphi workflow; repeat rounds connect anonymous feedback to independent estimates.

blocks.text: Experts review the anonymous feedback and revise their estimates independently. Rounds repeat; the coordinator compiles the final estimate.
No discussion between experts is allowed during the entire process, because some may be influenced by an experienced or senior estimator; comments in the summary stay anonymous.
COCOMO: the effort model
COCOMO (Constructive Cost Model), introduced by Boehm in 1981: Effort = a × (SIZE in KLOC)^b person-months. The constants a and b depend on the type of project.

blocks.caption: COCOMO: Effort = a × SIZE^b; a and b depend on project type.
blocks.alt: COCOMO: Effort = a × SIZE^b; a and b depend on project type.

blocks.text: COCOMO project types

rows: A well-understood application program; small team, mostly experienced
A mix of experienced and inexperienced people with limited experience building related systems
Strongly coupled with hardware; team may be large with many inexperienced people

blocks.caption: Figure 14. The three lecture categories: Organic, Semi-Detached and Embedded.

blocks.text: Effort depends not only on size but also on the type of project and the composition of the team; constants are lowest for organic (2.4, 1.05) and highest for embedded.
Seller Portal: estimate the size of seven modules

Not a straightforward system — modules interface with the main Amazon system and with banks for payments — so classified semi-detached (in some cases it could be embedded). LOC per module estimated from data of previous projects.

blocks.caption: Figure 15. Seven module estimates totaling 4 KLOC.

blocks.text: Cost drivers and effort adjustment factor

Required software reliability = very high (orders and money involved) → 1.40; database size = high → 1.08; application experience of the team = low → 1.13; programming language experience = high → 0.95. The 15 cost drivers are grouped into product, computer, personnel (and project) attributes; multiplying all of them gives the effort adjustment factor. Here only four are used for simplicity.

Other factors beyond size: people working on the project (experience with the framework/domain — e.g. e-commerce), technical attributes of the product (database size, complexity, reliability), tools and practices used by the team.
COCOMO worked example: slide values and corrected calculation

rows: Cost before adjustment (rounded initial effort), at ₹75,000 per person per month

blocks.text: Using the adjusted effort of approximately 23.0 person-months, the adjusted cost is 23.0 × ₹75,000 ≈ ₹17.25 lakh. The initial cost before adjustment is approximately ₹10.63 lakh without rounding effort to 14 PM.

The slide's 15.83 PM does not follow from 3.0 × 4^1.12 (which evaluates to ≈14.17). The method is unchanged; only the arithmetic differs. If asked to compute, use the correct value; if asked what the lecture states, it is 15.83 PM.
COCOMO summary

Determine the type of product → estimate LOC for each module → initial estimate → effort adjustment factor from the 15 cost drivers → overall estimate. The overall estimate depends on the LOC estimates, so get as much detail as possible and be aware of your biases.
A British Computer Society survey of more than 1000 projects found 92% of project managers made estimates using experience instead of formulas (A. Taylor, BCS Review, Jan 2000).
Why a schedule matters: a schedule helps the project manager monitor the timely completion of each task, and take corrective action if the project falls behind.
The eight scheduling activities

blocks.caption: Figure 16. The eight principal steps of project scheduling.

blocks.text: Work Breakdown Structure (WBS)
The root is the project. Each node is broken into children; each leaf is a task that can be allocated to a developer and scheduled, roughly two weeks of work.
Seller Portal WBS

The Seller Portal is broken into Requirement Gathering and Analysis, Design and Development. Requirements includes gathering requirements and creating an SRS. Design includes the component diagram, database schema and user interface. Development includes catalogue management, inventory management and order tracking.

blocks.caption: Seller Portal WBS.

blocks.text: From WBS to activity network
Leaf nodes of the WBS become nodes of the activity network. The activity network shows dependencies and durations of tasks.

blocks.caption: WBS leaf nodes become activity network nodes: dependencies are shown here; Figure 20 and the table add task durations.
blocks.alt: WBS leaf nodes become activity network nodes.

blocks.caption: Figure 20. The lecture’s nine-task Seller Portal dependency network.

blocks.text: Gantt chart

A special type of bar chart: each bar is an activity, its length proportional to the planned duration. In the Seller Portal, user interface and database schema start together (UI takes longer); catalogue, inventory and order tracking happen one after the other; then payment, sales and customer feedback happen in parallel.

blocks.caption: Seller Portal Gantt chart (days).

blocks.text: Representations like the Gantt chart help all members of the team be aware of the schedule.
Critical path
The critical path is a chain of tasks that determines the duration of the project.

A risk is a possible future unfavorable event. It is worth managing before it happens: after a problem has already caused a delay, the team is responding to an incident rather than anticipating a risk.
Why risks are harder to see in software

The lecture defines a project risk as an anticipated unfavorable event that may occur during development. When a house is built, the construction manager can see every stage — foundation, slabs, frame, roofing, interiors, painting — and assess and control progress. Software is intangible, so it is difficult to control something we cannot see.

blocks.caption: Figure 23. Anticipated obstacles in a software project versus visible construction progress.

blocks.text: Examples include a syntax error that disrupts a larger system, vulnerable components, disagreements within the development team and unexpected delays. The project manager identifies, assesses, mitigates and continues monitoring such risks rather than assuming everything will go according to plan.
Three categories: technical, project and business

Technical risks are risks related to the technical aspects of the project, arising from the development team's insufficient knowledge about the product; they can occur at any stage — requirements, design, implementation, testing or maintenance. Project risks occur due to problems in budget, schedule, personnel, resources and customer-related problems — all non-technical risks are project risks. Business risks are risks which can harm the business aspects of the software product.

blocks.caption: Figure 24. Technical, project and business risk classifications.

blocks.text: Technical risk: misunderstood requirements

The team may develop the wrong functions or user interfaces, mainly because the requirements received from the client are ambiguous or incomplete. Ambiguity or incompleteness in requirements can cause incorrect user interfaces, workflows and implemented features.

blocks.caption: Figure 25. Seller Portal before and after requirements clarification.

blocks.text: The mitigation described in the lecture is regular client communication and early prototypes. Demonstrate a small version, ask stakeholders whether it matches their needs, and refine before investing heavily in the wrong design.
Technical risk: external software components

External libraries, cloud services and vendor modules can be unreliable, incompatible, slow or vulnerable. Depending on a component transfers some work to another supplier, but it also creates a risk outside the team’s direct control.

blocks.caption: Figure 26. A component failure pathway with benchmark, inspection and suitability checks.

blocks.text: Benchmark candidate components and inspect them periodically.
Project risks: slippage, missing expertise, staff departures

If milestones slip, a project manager can create smaller checkpoints, communicate the revised status promptly and use frequent iterations to reveal delay early. Missing domain knowledge—for example, unfamiliarity with an e-commerce payments process—can be addressed by experienced staff or selectively outsourcing relevant modules.

blocks.caption: Figure 27. Three project risks paired with practical mitigation techniques.

blocks.text: Personnel shortfall occurs when key people leave or become unavailable. Cross-training and shared technical knowledge reduce dependence on one developer. The lecture uses the specialised payment-gateway module as an example where more than one trained person would help reduce continuity risk.
Business risks: competition and gold plating

A business product can be completed successfully from an engineering viewpoint and still fail commercially if it is uncompetitive. Market research and comparison with other products help identify what users actually value and where meaningful gaps remain.

blocks.caption: Figure 28. Poor competitiveness and low-value extra functionality.

blocks.text: Gold plating means adding attractive but unnecessary features that the customer has not requested. Extra widgets and reports can consume time, money and attention. Discuss them with the client and assess their costs against benefits before including them.
Risk probability, impact and score

The project manager asks everyone in the team for the worst-case scenario, then creates a risk table; probability P is assigned from 0 to 100%. Impact: 1 negligible, 2 marginal, 3 critical, 4 catastrophic.

blocks.caption: Figure 29. Risk probability multiplied by the stated impact category.

blocks.text: Risk = P × I. For schedule slippage with P = 60% = 0.60 and impact = 3, Risk = 1.8. Sort risks in descending order.
Seller Portal risk table: allocate attention

The lecture’s illustrative risk table gives schedule slippage P=60%, I=3; lack of experience P=60%, I=3; personnel shortfall P=40%, I=3; and database scale risk P=20%, I=2. Their scores are respectively 1.8, 1.8, 1.2 and 0.4.

blocks.caption: Seller Portal risk table, sorted by risk.
blocks.alt: Seller Portal risk table, sorted by risk.

blocks.text: You cannot anticipate every risk, so focus on the most important ones — e.g. mitigate schedule slippage with milestones and regular meetings with the team and clients, and lack of experience by hiring the right people from within or outside the company.
Quick recall
A risk is a possible future unfavorable event, not simply a defect already observed.
Identify the category, mitigation, likelihood and potential impact of each important risk.
Risk scores prioritize attention; they are not exact measurements of monetary loss.
Agile iterations

Software is developed in iterations of typically 1–2 weeks; certain user stories are implemented in each iteration, and user stories are prioritized for the next iteration. The team works closely with customers, demonstrates working functionality and refines requirements.

blocks.caption: Figure 31. Repeated short iterations and progressively richer Seller Portal versions.
blocks.alt: Illustration: Section 5 · Project Management in Agile

blocks.text: Scrum team and roles

Scrum is one framework for organising development in the team. At its heart is the sprint — a short, time-boxed period when a Scrum team works to complete a set amount of work; the product is built in a series of sprints.
Team size roughly 4 to 9 people (varies by company).

rows: Whoever is required to complete the work in that sprint (designers, developers, testers).

Interfaces between the client and the development team; ensures the team delivers the most value to the client; takes into account other stakeholders and constraints (developers', technology) and communicates them to the client; prioritizes the work to be done in a particular sprint using inputs from clients and the team.

Ensures all Scrum activities are done well; helps the product owner define value and the development team deliver it; serves the organization by helping it understand Scrum and creating an environment that supports it.

blocks.caption: Figure 32. Three collaborating Scrum roles, with a cross-functional development team.
blocks.alt: Illustration: Section 5 · Project Management in Agile

blocks.text: Product backlog and sprint planning

A prioritized list of work for the development team, derived from user stories and requirements; the most important items are at the top. Who prioritizes it? Not the product owner alone — in the sprint planning meeting all team members collectively decide which items will be worked on in the sprint.

rows: Catalogue: a add, b edit, c delete
Inventory: a add, b edit, c delete

blocks.text: EXAMPLE  Product Owner: the client wants catalogue and inventory management. Developers: it is not possible to complete both. The team agrees on 1a (Add catalogue item) and 2a (Add inventory item).

blocks.caption: Backlog → sprint planning → Sprint 1 (1a, 2a).

blocks.text: Tools like JIRA let you create a backlog, create sprints, move items into a sprint, set a timeline and assign stories to people.
Sprint planning: what work, and how

Sprint Planning is a collaborative meeting involving the Product Owner, Scrum Master and Development Team. What work can get done in this sprint? How will the chosen work get done? About 2 hours per week of iteration.

blocks.caption: Sprint planning: what work, and how.
blocks.alt: Sprint planning: what work, and how.

blocks.text: Daily scrum

Participants: development team, scrum master and product manager. Three questions: What did I work on yesterday? What am I working on today? What issues are blocking me? It strengthens the team because everyone shares their progress.

blocks.caption: Figure 35. Daily coordination beside a small task board and a visible blocker.
blocks.alt: Illustration: Section 5 · Project Management in Agile

blocks.text: Sprint review and retrospective
Sprint review: the team demonstrates what it completed; items move from To-Do/In Progress to Done.

blocks.caption: Figure 36. Two different end-of-sprint meetings and their outcomes.
blocks.alt: Illustration: Section 5 · Project Management in Agile

blocks.text: Sprint retrospective: evaluate team dynamics, processes and tools; what went well, what did not and why; create and implement a plan to improve.
Story points and velocity

The lecture first estimates 10 user stories at 2 stories per sprint: 5 sprints, or 10 weeks with two-week sprints. This assumes comparable effort per story; unequal story difficulty makes counting stories alone unreliable.
Rate each user story by difficulty: 1 straightforward, 2 medium, 3 very complex. Counting stories alone does not account for differences in difficulty.

blocks.caption: Figure 37. Two sprints with three stories each but different point totals.
blocks.alt: Illustration: Section 5 · Project Management in Agile

blocks.text: Velocity = number of points completed per iteration/sprint. Add catalogue (2 points) + Add inventory item (2 points) completed in sprint 1 → velocity = 4. In the next iteration the team can take four 1-point stories, because it can complete 4 points per sprint.

blocks.caption: Velocity = points completed per sprint.

blocks.text: Plan and Document versus Agile scheduling

blocks.caption: Plan and Document: early tasks, Gantt charts and milestones; Agile: user stories, points and velocity.
blocks.alt: Plan and Document: early tasks, Gantt charts and milestones; Agile: user stories, points and velocity.

blocks.text: The lecture demonstrates Pivotal Tracker, a tool for tracking user stories and velocity, including signing up and creating a project. This is a historical demonstration: the service ended on 30 April 2025.
Set up a project and understand its workspace

The tutorial begins by creating a project named “IIT Software Engineering Project.” It shows the current iteration or prioritized backlog, an Icebox of unprioritized ideas, the iteration-length setting and team membership. The example uses an iteration length of two weeks.

blocks.caption: Workspace: current iteration, Icebox, epics.

blocks.text: The Icebox is a holding place for stories that are not yet selected or prioritized. The working backlog contains stories that the team has considered for near-term development. Team members can be invited so responsibility and progress are visible within the tool.
Create a feature story with tasks and links

The tutorial creates a feature story such as “Add Catalogue Item.” It selects a feature type, assigns an illustrative 2 story points and priority, and adds a description, labels, optional source-code links or attachments, tasks and comments. Two example tasks are “Create and Review UI Screen” and “Create Catalogue Database Table.”

blocks.caption: Figure 41. An illustrative feature-story form with points, tasks, owner, links and comments.

blocks.text: A story records user-facing functionality; its tasks describe the concrete work required to implement it. An owner is responsible for progressing the assigned story. Saving a story records the plan—it does not mean implementation is finished, delivered or accepted.
Epics group related user stories

An epic is a collection of related stories describing a broader area of functionality. The tutorial groups Add/Edit/View/Delete Catalogue Item stories under the Catalogue Management epic, while Add Inventory Item is linked to the Inventory Management epic.

blocks.caption: Figure 42. Catalogue and inventory epics containing their related stories.

blocks.text: An epic is not the same as a task checklist. A user story delivers a meaningful slice of capability, whereas a task may be a database table, UI implementation or testing step needed to complete the story. Grouping stories helps the team see progress across a larger feature.
Move ideas from Icebox to planned work

Customer feedback and order tracking are added to the Icebox as ideas to implement in the future. The current iteration holds Add catalogue item and Add inventory item (feature, high priority, 2 points each); velocity set to 4.

blocks.caption: Icebox ideas vs current iteration (velocity 4).

blocks.text: Feature-story lifecycle: start through acceptance

A feature story moves from Not Started to Started while a developer works on it. The developer documents work, completes tasks and marks the story Finished. Clicking Deliver sends a status update to the product owner, who reviews comments/links and accepts or rejects the story.

blocks.caption: Figure 44. Delivered stories are reviewed; rejected work returns to development.

blocks.text: The Product Owner checks the functionality, notes and links and can Accept or Reject. Acceptance records that the delivered story meets expectations. Rejection returns it for further development; the developer restarts work, corrects problems and submits it again. “Finished by developer” and “Accepted by Product Owner” are different milestones.
When a delivered story is rejected

The lecture demonstrates the Product Owner rejecting “Add Catalogue Item” with feedback such as failing test cases and too many bugs. The developer reads the comments, fixes the implementation, retests the affected scenarios and delivers the story again.

blocks.caption: Figure 45. A rejection, repair, retest and redelivery cycle.

blocks.text: The story should remain unaccepted until the Product Owner reviews the improved delivery. Comments, linked code and task history create an audit trail of what was attempted and what changed. This makes the tool valuable for team coordination rather than just counting checkboxes.
Analytics: improve the next iteration

The tutorial also discusses analytics including accepted stories, rejection rate, story cycle time and recent epics. The team can use these to ask whether stories are waiting too long for review, whether feedback commonly triggers rework or whether work is moving steadily.

blocks.caption: Figure 46. Illustrative project analytics and feedback-informed iteration planning.

blocks.text: Quick recall
Icebox ideas are not the same as prioritized current-iteration stories.
Stories can carry types, points, labels, tasks, comments, code links and owners.
Epic = group of related stories; story = user-facing capability; task = implementation step.
Finish → Deliver → Product Owner accepts or rejects; rejected stories require rework.

blocks.text: Five practice questions with answers
1. A system needs 5,000 LOC. What is its size?
Answer: 5 KLOC. This estimates size, not person-month effort.
2. An illustration shows 4 developers working for 3 months. What is the nominal effort?
Answer: 4 × 3 = 12 person-months, assuming comparable full-time effort.
3. A risk has P=40% and impact=3. What is its risk score?
Answer: 0.40 × 3 = 1.2; it is neither 120% nor ₹1.2.
4. A sprint completes stories worth 2, 1 and 3 points. What is observed velocity?
Answer: 2 + 1 + 3 = 6 points for that sprint.
5. In Delphi, after anonymous summary feedback, which stage repeats?
Answer: The experts independently submit revised estimates; the final estimate does not trigger the loop.
